Bliss

/blis/ — rhymes with kiss · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bliss is a feeling of complete happiness and contentment, as if nothing could be better in that moment.

Floating in the warm lagoon, she felt a moment of pure bliss.

Worked Example

Wrapped in a cozy blanket with hot tea after a stressful week, she sank into complete bliss—nothing else mattered and nothing more was needed.

Bliss is the perfect word because it names that sense of total contentment where you feel like you want for nothing more in that moment. Happiness would miss the profound sense of being completely satisfied and at peace.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

peace: Peace is calm freedom from worry, noise, and conflict — the storm stops, the arguing ends, the mind quiets. It describes what is absent. Bliss describes what is present: happiness so complete that nothing could make the moment better. An empty, quiet afternoon brings peace; a perfect one brings bliss.

ecstasy: Ecstasy is joy at explosive intensity — leaping, shouting, swept off your feet, like fans when the winning goal lands. Bliss is just as complete but calm: a deep, serene contentment with nothing missing. Ecstasy surges and burns out; bliss settles over you and feels like it could last forever.

rapture: Rapture is being utterly carried away by delight — so absorbed in music or a starry sky that the rest of the world disappears. It is joy with your attention captured. Bliss is quieter: total, settled contentment where nothing needs to change. Rapture seizes you; bliss simply fills you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

torment: severe suffering of body or mind

misery: deep, ongoing unhappiness and distress

Where it sits · how complete the joy feels — discontent → contentment → happiness → bliss

discontent vs. bliss: Discontent is the opposite end of this scale from bliss: it is restless dissatisfaction with things as they are, while bliss is such perfect happiness that nothing feels missing.

contentment vs. bliss: Contentment is pleasant but much weaker than bliss — contentment says 'this is fine,' while bliss says 'nothing in the world could possibly be better than this.'

happiness vs. bliss: Happiness is strong, yet bliss goes further: happiness is feeling genuinely glad, while bliss is complete, wrap-around happiness without a single flaw.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bliss (blīþs)

Root — bliss (blīþs): gentle joy, merriment (related to blithe) (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Bliss is a single Old English root, blīþs, built on blīþe ('gentle, kind, joyous') — the whole word has meant perfect, glowing happiness for over a thousand years.

Use the root in a new word: blissful

Use the root in a new word: blissful: The honeymooners spent a blissful week on the quiet island, every day full of the perfect, complete happiness that bliss names.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Bliss describes that rare, perfect moment when nothing could be better—when you're not just happy but completely, serenely satisfied. Use it for moments of pure contentment: relaxing by the ocean, a perfect afternoon, total peace. For everyday happiness, 'happiness' or 'contentment' usually works better.
